newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Foiled plot mars Nicaragua presidential inauguration.
newsitem.headline: Foiled plot mars Nicaragua presidential inauguration.

text.p: Right-winger Arnoldo Aleman, taking the oath as Nicaragua's president on Friday, held out an olive branch to his sworn enemies, the Sandinistas, to quell a growing threat of social unrest from the left.
But hopes the gesture would calm a notoriously divided country were shattered when police said they had arrested two men who planned a dynamite attack on the new president.
"We have arrested two men, one of whom has been identified as a retired police officer, who were carrying dynamite ready to explode," police spokesman Capt. Justo Zamora told Reuters.
Zamora said the men, arrested in the capital Managua, had confessed they were going to use the dynamite against Aleman. He had no further details.
Ironically, during his inauguration speech Aleman had opened the door to his political enemies.

"I extend the fraternal, open and frank hand of friendship and invite our political competitors, particularly the FSLN (Sandinista National Liberation Front) to dialogue," a beaming Aleman said to 10,000 well-wishers and seven Latin American presidents under the scorching sun in the national stadium.
But the Sandinistas, who led Nicaragua through revolutionary rule between 1979-1990, boycotted the ceremony.

Aleman's inauguration was the first time in modern Nicaraguan history that one elected, civilian government handed power to another and his supporters celebrated exuberantly, letting off bursts of blue and white balloons.

Aleman, a 50-year-old lawyer and coffee grower who relishes his nickname "Fatman", rolled into the half-filled stadium in his open-topped red Mercedes-Benz, dubbed the "Fatmobile" by his supporters in the press.

Amid the booming of cannons, National Assembly president Ivan Escobar Fornos placed the blue-and-white presidential sash over the burly shoulders of Aleman, who has promised a new era of democracy and prosperity to Nicaragua, the second poorest country in the Americas after Haiti.

Aleman urged Nicaraguans to "forgive and forget" those responsible for the country's war-ravaged, authoritarian past that it only begun to shake off when outgoing president Violeta Chamorro, 67, defeated the Sandinistas in 1990.
"We will not return to the past, the long, dark night is over for Nicaragua," Aleman said.

Chamorro, an ailing, silver-haired former housewife who had been Latin America's only female head of state, was greeted with heartfelt cheering when she entered the stadium, using a walking stick on her last day in office.

The ceremony coincided with the 19th anniversary of the assassination of her husband, newspaper publisher Pedro Joaquin Chamorro. His death helped spark the Sandinista uprising that toppled dictator Anastasio Somoza in 1979.
A dark-suited Aleman said his government would work for the 70 percent of Nicaraguans who live in grinding poverty.
"We open a new period of peace, hope and prosperity, and will focus the best of our abilities, creativity and resources to solving the most urgent needs of the people," he said.
But amid the jubilation an undercurrent of fear remained as angry Sandinista leftists warned of street protests, and rumblings of violence were heard in the countryside.
The Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua with Soviet and Cuban backing, used their muscle to frustrate the Chamorro government in its early years.

In a chilling reminder of past violence, an unknown armed group on Thursday ambushed an army patrol, killing six Nicaraguan soldiers -- including a major and two captains -- in the central province of Matagalpa, police said.

Despite the end of Nicaragua's civil war between the Sandinistas and U.S.-backed Contra rebels in the 1980s, Aleman's Liberal Alliance and the Sandinistas remain bitter enemies and analysts have warned that clashes between the two in coming years could scare away much-needed investment.
This hostility boiled over on Thursday when the Sandinistas stormed out of the National Assembly's inaugural session, angered by a Supreme Electoral Council ruling on vote-taking in parliament.

The day before, the Supreme Court had struck down 80 Sandinista-sponsored laws in a ruling former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega described as a "coup d'etat" and "a death sentence for the rule of law."
With the Liberals controlling the government, parliament and judiciary, Sandinistas said they would have to take their protests to the streets.
